spec.hypothesis: The scaled logistic baseline reached macro_f1 0.547 versus 0.202 for the dummy, so linear signal is strong, but macro_f1 trails accuracy (0.574) with imbalanced classes (605/1193/1394), and features span very different scales/ranges. A nonlinear tree model should capture interactions and threshold effects that the linear model misses; ExtraTrees with bounded depth (8) and sqrt feature sampling offers a good bias-variance tradeoff on this 3192-row, 12-feature set and is a distinct model family from the linear baseline.

Logistic regression remains the strongest model so far (macro_f1 0.547), while the tuned ExtraTrees underperformed (0.504), suggesting the signal is largely linear and tree interactions add noise. However, macro_f1 still trails accuracy (0.574), indicating the minority classes are underpredicted under imbalance (605/1193/1394). Since the linear structure already serves the data well, the next lever is class imbalance: keeping the proven scaled-median logistic setup with C=1.0 but adding balanced class weights should lift minority-class recall and thus macro_f1 without changing the model family or discarding the linear signal.

Unregularized logistic (C=1.0) is still the best result (macro_f1 0.547); balanced weighting at C=1.0 dropped to 0.536 and ExtraTrees underperformed (0.504), confirming signal is largely linear and features vary widely in scale (e.g. std of col7 ~0.003 vs col6 ~56.7), so scaling matters. Moving to weaker regularization C=10.0 keeps the proven scaled-median setup and nearest-neighbor preprocessing but lets the linear boundary fit sharper class distinctions, which may lift macro_f1 on the imbalanced 3-class problem without an over-regularization penalty at C=1.0.

Logistic regression with scaled-median preprocessing dominates: C=1.0 gave macro_f1 0.547 and C=10.0 improved further to 0.551, while class-weight balancing (0.536) and ExtraTrees (0.504) both hurt, confirming a largely linear signal with weak over-regularization cost. Since increasing C from 1 to 10 helped, continuing in the same direction is the most evidence-consistent next step, but the candidate space has no logistic row beyond C=10.0 with null class_weight. The nearest unexplored multi-class nonlinear option is boosted trees: histogram gradient boosting with a moderate 0.1 learning rate can capture any residual interactions while its shrinkage controls overfitting, exploiting the categorical column without abandoning the scaled-median pipeline.

Evidence shows a largely linear signal: logistic C=10.0 (0.551) and C=1.0 (0.547) lead, while ExtraTrees (0.504) and balanced weighting (0.536) hurt. HistGradientBoosting at lr 0.1 already matched the best logistic (0.552), suggesting mild nonlinear gains are accessible. Since no logistic candidate beyond C=10.0 with null class_weight remains untried, the least-redundant novel exploration in the boosted family is CatBoost, which handles the categorical column natively and generally differs from histogram GB in regularization/leaf growth. depth 4 with 200 iterations, lr 0.1, l2 3.0, no class weights keeps settings closest to the best-performing unweighted configurations and avoids the imbalance handling that previously degraded results.

CatBoost depth 4 with unweighted loss is the clear leader (macro_f1 0.570), beating linear (0.551) and histogram GB (0.552), while ExtraTrees (0.504) and balanced class weights (0.536) hurt. Boosting clearly extracts useful nonlinearity that linear models miss. Depth 4 worked; the untried depth-6 CatBoost with identical otherwise-default settings is the natural next step to test whether greater tree depth captures additional interactions without destabilizing. All tried balance-weight variants degraded results, so keep null class weights and the proven scaled-median pipeline.
